title: Emotional Intelligence
paragraphs: Emotional intelligence (EQ) is the ability to understand and manage your own emotions, and to understand the emotions of others. In the modern world, EQ is considered just as important as academic intelligence (IQ).

People with high emotional intelligence enjoy communicating with others. They don't mind dealing with difficult situations because they know how to stay calm. They avoid reacting with anger and instead think before they speak.

Psychologist Dr. Daniel Goleman identified five key parts of EQ: self-awareness (knowing your feelings), self-regulation (controlling reactions), motivation (staying focused on goals), empathy (understanding others), and social skills (building relationships).

At WKU, Dr. Akhmetov often mentions EQ in his workshops. 'Students who develop emotional intelligence do better in group projects,' he says. 'They know when to speak and when to listen. They appreciate different perspectives.'

You can practise EQ every day. Start by noticing your emotions without judging them. Try writing in a journal. Avoid using your phone when you feel bored — instead, think about what you actually feel. Consider talking to someone you trust when you feel confused or sad.
Emotional intelligence is not a fixed trait — it grows with practice. Every time you choose empathy over anger, every time you decide to listen instead of argue, you are building your EQ.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Dr. Akhmetov, how do I improve my emotional intelligence?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: Start by noticing your emotions. Don't judge them — just name them.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I often feel frustrated during group work. Is that bad?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: Not at all. Recognising frustration is step one. Avoiding a reaction is step two.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I enjoy working alone, but I know I need to practise working in teams.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: That's excellent self-awareness, Amir. Keep practising.
